title: Armorum iudicium. Aiax
titleEn: Ulysses Counts His Services — Metamorphoses XIII.140–267
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Ulysses answers Ajax's claim of birth, counting his own descent from Jupiter through Laertes and Arcesius, and a second nobility from the Cyllenian god on his mother's side, and asks that the case be weighed on deserts rather than kinship. He tells how Achilles was hidden in a girl's dress until he laid arms among the women's wares and sent the brave man off to brave work, and on that ground claims Achilles' victories as his own. He recounts the becalmed fleet at Aulis and the daughter whom hard oracles demanded, the embassy into the council-house of Troy, the ambushes and the counsel of the long siege, the night he killed Dolon and destroyed Rhesus in his own camp, and the men he cut down beneath the walls. He ends by drawing his clothing down to show his wounds, and says that Telamon's son has spent no blood on his comrades and carries a body without a wound.

sentences.t:
Nam genus et proavos et quae non fecimus ipsi,
vix ea nostra voco;
sentences.l: For lineage and forefathers and the things which we ourselves did not do — these I scarcely call ours;
sentences.i: For birth and ancestry, and whatever we did not do ourselves — I hardly call such things our own;
sentences.n: The neuter ‘ea’ gathers up what has gone before — ‘genus’, ‘proavos’ and the relative clause ‘quae non fecimus ipsi’ — and carries them into the main clause as the object of ‘voco’; Latin often sets out a list and then resumes it with a pronoun. ‘nostra’ is a predicate accusative with ‘voco’, “call them ours”. Ulysses opens his reply by giving away the ground of birth, so that he can take it back in the next breath.

sentences.t:
sed enim quia rettulit Aiax
esse Iovis pronepos, nostri quoque sanguinis auctor
Iuppiter est, totidemque gradus distamus ab illo.
sentences.l: but in fact, since Ajax has brought up that he is a great-grandson of Jupiter, of our blood too Jupiter is the founder, and by just as many steps are we distant from him.
sentences.i: But since Ajax has raised the matter of being Jupiter's great-grandson — Jupiter founded my blood as well, and I stand at exactly the same remove from him.
sentences.n: ‘pronepos’ is nominative, not accusative: in an indirect statement whose subject is the same as the reporting verb's, Latin keeps the nominative, so ‘rettulit ... esse Iovis pronepos’ is “he reported that he was Jupiter's great-grandson”. ‘totidem gradus’ is an accusative of extent, “by so many steps”. ‘nostri’ and ‘distamus’ are the plural Ulysses uses of himself, which runs through the whole speech beside a first-person singular.

sentences.t:
Nam mihi Laertes pater est, Arcesius illi,
Iuppiter huic, neque in his quisquam damnatus et exsul.
sentences.l: For to me Laertes is father, to him Arcesius, to this one Jupiter — and among these there is not anyone condemned and an exile.
sentences.i: For my father is Laertes, his father Arcesius, and his father Jupiter — and not one of them a man condemned and banished.
sentences.n: The dative of possession three times over — ‘mihi’, ‘illi’, ‘huic’ — with ‘est’ heard again in the second and third: Latin gives a pedigree by saying “to X there is a father Y”. The last clause is a thrust, not a boast: it prepares the charge of ‘fraterni sanguinis’ at 149, where Ulysses says his own father has no brother's blood on him.

sentences.t:
Est quoque per matrem Cyllenius addita nobis
altera nobilitas: deus est in utroque parente.
sentences.l: There is also, through my mother, the Cyllenian — a second nobility added to us: a god is in each parent.
sentences.i: On my mother's side too there is the god of Cyllene — a second nobility added to me: there is a god on both sides of my house.
sentences.n: ‘Cyllenius’ is Mercury, named from Mount Cyllene in Arcadia; Ulysses' mother was the daughter of Autolycus, Mercury's son. ‘addita nobis altera nobilitas’ stands in apposition to the whole clause before it — the fact that there is a Cyllenian on the mother's side is the second nobility. ‘in utroque parente’ is “in each of the two parents”, that is, on both sides.

sentences.t:
Sed neque materno quod sum generosior ortu,
nec mihi quod pater est fraterni sanguinis insons,
proposita arma peto:
sentences.l: But neither because I am nobler by my mother's descent, nor because I have a father innocent of a brother's blood, do I seek the arms set out:
sentences.i: But it is not because my mother's line is the nobler, nor because my father has no brother's blood on him, that I claim the arms laid before us:
sentences.n: Two ‘quod’ clauses, both “because”, hang on ‘peto’, and ‘neque ... nec’ denies the ground rather than the act — he does seek the arms, only not on those terms. ‘mihi’ is again the dative of possession, “I have a father”. ‘insons’ takes a genitive of the charge, as Latin verbs of accusing and acquitting do. ‘proposita’ is the word for a prize set out for a contest.

sentences.t:
meritis expendite causam,
dummodo, quod fratres Telamon Peleusque fuerunt,
Aiacis meritum non sit nec sanguinis ordo,
sentences.l: weigh the case by deserts, provided only that this — that Telamon and Peleus were brothers — not be Ajax's merit, nor the order of blood,
sentences.i: weigh the case on deserts, provided only that the brotherhood of Telamon and Peleus count as no merit of Ajax's, nor the order of kinship,
sentences.n: ‘dummodo’ with the subjunctive states a proviso, “on this one condition, that…”, and governs ‘sit’ here and ‘quaeratur’ in the next unit. The noun clause ‘quod fratres Telamon Peleusque fuerunt’ is the subject of ‘sit’: the fact of the brotherhood is what must not count. Telamon was Ajax's father and Peleus Achilles', and that kinship is the whole of Ajax's claim by blood.

sentences.t: sed virtutis honor spoliis quaeratur in istis!
sentences.l: but let the prize of valour be sought in those spoils there!
sentences.i: but let it be the reward of valour that is looked for in those spoils!
sentences.n: ‘iste’ points at what is in view or belongs to the person addressed; here the arms displayed before the assembly. ‘quaeratur’ is still under the ‘dummodo’ of 151, so this is the positive half of the same proviso. ‘virtutis honor’ is the term Ulysses wants the case tried on, set directly against ‘sanguinis ordo’ in the line before.

sentences.t:
Aut si proximitas primusque requiritur heres,
est genitor Peleus, est Pyrrhus filius illi.
sentences.l: Or if nearness of kin and the first heir is what is looked for, there is a father Peleus, there is a son Pyrrhus, to him.
sentences.i: Or if it is next-of-kin and the first heir that is wanted — Peleus is his father, Pyrrhus his son.
sentences.n: ‘requiritur’ is singular though it has two subjects, ‘proximitas’ and ‘heres’; Latin regularly lets one singular verb serve a pair like this. ‘illi’ is a dative of possession serving both halves: Achilles has a father and a son, and both stand nearer in law than a cousin does. Pyrrhus is Achilles' son, reared on Scyros; Peleus' kingdom is Phthia, and the next line sends the arms to both places.

sentences.t: Quis locus Aiaci? Phthiam haec Scyrumve ferantur!
sentences.l: What place is there for Ajax? Let these things be carried to Phthia or to Scyros!
sentences.i: What standing has Ajax here? Let the arms go to Phthia, then, or to Scyros!
sentences.n: ‘Phthiam’ and ‘Scyrum’ are accusatives of the goal of motion with no preposition, the regular usage with names of towns and small islands. ‘haec’ is the arms. ‘ferantur’ is a jussive subjunctive, and the order is sarcastic: Ulysses is not proposing it, he is showing where Ajax's own principle would send the prize.

sentences.t:
Nec minus est isto Teucer patruelis Achilli:
num petit ille tamen? num si petat, auferat illa?
sentences.l: Nor is Teucer less a cousin to Achilles than that man there: does he for all that seek them? and if he should seek, would he carry them off?
sentences.i: And Teucer is no less Achilles' cousin than that fellow is — yet does he put in a claim? And if he did, would he win them?
sentences.n: ‘isto’ is an ablative of comparison, “than that man of yours”, and it is contemptuous — Ajax. ‘Achilli’ is a dative with ‘patruelis’. ‘num’ twice over expects the answer “no”. ‘si petat ... auferat’ is a pair of present subjunctives, the future-less-vivid condition: “if he should seek, would he carry off”. Teucer was Ajax's own half-brother, Telamon's son, so the cousinship Ajax rests on is Teucer's too.

sentences.l: Therefore, since a bare contest of deeds is being held: I have indeed done more than what it would be ready to hand for me to gather up in words;
sentences.i: So then, since it is a plain contest of deeds: I have done more than I could readily set out in speech;
sentences.n: ‘in promptu esse’ is “to be ready to hand, be easy”, so ‘quam quae comprendere dictis in promptu mihi sit’ is “than such things as it would be easy for me to gather into words”; ‘sit’ is a generic subjunctive after ‘quam quae’. ‘nudum certamen operum’ is “a bare contest of deeds”, stripped of the birth-claims he has just set aside — and the modesty is a device, since the catalogue follows anyway.

sentences.t: rerum tamen ordine ducar.
sentences.l: yet I shall be led by the order of events.
sentences.i: still, I shall let the order of events lead me.
sentences.n: ‘ducar’ is future passive, “I shall be led”, and the passive is the point: the speaker presents himself as carried along by his material rather than choosing what to boast of. ‘rerum ordine’ is an ablative of means.

sentences.t:
Praescia venturi genetrix Nereia leti
dissimulat cultu natum, et deceperat omnes,
in quibus Aiacem, sumptae fallacia vestis.
sentences.l: His Nereid mother, foreknowing the death that was coming, disguises her son by his dress, and the deceit of the clothing taken on had deceived everyone — among them Ajax.
sentences.i: His mother, the Nereid, knowing beforehand the death that was to come, hid her son in a dress, and the trick of the borrowed clothes had taken in everyone — Ajax among them.
sentences.n: Thetis, a daughter of Nereus, hid the boy Achilles among the girls because she knew what awaited him at Troy. ‘praescia venturi ... leti’ takes an objective genitive, with the future participle ‘venturi’ agreeing with ‘leti’, “of the death about to come”. ‘dissimulat’ is a historic present standing beside the pluperfect ‘deceperat’, which reaches back behind it. ‘in quibus Aiacem’ is elliptical — the verb “it had deceived” is heard again — and the sneer is the whole reason the clause exists.

sentences.t:
Arma ego femineis animum motura virilem
mercibus inserui, neque adhuc proiecerat heros
virgineos habitus,
sentences.l: I among womanly wares slipped in arms that were going to stir a manly spirit, and the hero had not yet thrown off his maiden's clothing,
sentences.i: I planted among the women's goods arms that were bound to move a man's heart; and the hero had not yet flung off his girl's dress,
sentences.n: ‘motura’ is a future participle used of a destined effect — “arms that would stir” — agreeing with ‘arma’ and governing ‘animum virilem’; ‘inserui’ takes the dative ‘mercibus’. The word order does the work: ‘femineis’ (165) waits for ‘mercibus’ (166) across the line-end, and inside that frame sits ‘animum ... virilem’ with ‘motura’ between, so the manly spirit lies in the middle of the women's goods. ‘heros’ is a Greek loan-word and keeps its Greek declension in Latin.

sentences.t:
cum parmam hastamque tenenti
“nate dea,” dixi “tibi se peritura reservant
Pergama!
sentences.l: when, to him as he held a shield and a spear, I said, “Goddess-born one,” — “for you the Pergama, doomed to perish, are keeping themselves!
sentences.i: when I said to him, as he held shield and spear: “Son of a goddess — Pergamum is keeping itself for you, and it is doomed to fall!
sentences.n: ‘nate dea’ is a vocative with an ablative of origin, “born from a goddess”. ‘tenenti’ is a dative participle with no noun expressed, “to him as he held”. ‘Pergama’ is neuter plural, the citadel of Troy standing for the city, and ‘peritura’ is the future participle again, “about to perish”. This is Ulysses quoting his own words inside his speech: the edition opens the quotation at ‘nate dea’, breaks it to insert ‘dixi’, and opens it again at ‘tibi’.

sentences.t: quid dubitas ingentem evertere Troiam?”
sentences.l: why do you hesitate to overturn mighty Troy?”
sentences.i: why do you hold back from overthrowing great Troy?”
sentences.n: ‘dubito’ with an infinitive is “hesitate to”, not “doubt that”. The closing quotation mark ends the words Ulysses reports himself as having spoken; from the next line he is in his own voice again, still inside the speech he is making now.

sentences.t: iniecique manum fortemque ad fortia misi.
sentences.l: and I laid my hand on him and sent the brave man to brave things.
sentences.i: and I laid a hand on him and sent a brave man to brave work.
sentences.n: ‘manum inicere’ is the formal Roman act of laying hands on a person or thing to claim it as one's own before a magistrate. Ulysses reaches for the legal phrase deliberately: the whole argument that follows is that Achilles was his acquisition. ‘fortem ... ad fortia’ plays a masculine adjective used as a noun, “the brave man”, against a neuter plural, “brave deeds”.

sentences.t:
Ergo opera illius mea sunt: ego Telephon hasta
pugnantem domui, victum orantemque refeci;
sentences.l: Therefore his works are mine: I tamed Telephus, as he fought, with the spear; beaten and pleading, I made him whole again;
sentences.i: So his deeds are mine: I broke Telephus in the fighting with the spear, and healed him again when he was beaten and begging;
sentences.n: ‘Telephon’ is a Greek accusative in ‘-on’, kept as Greek. ‘domui’ is the perfect of ‘domo’, “I tamed”, and ‘pugnantem’, ‘victum’ and ‘orantem’ are three participles all agreeing with ‘Telephon’. The first person is the claim of 171 pressed as far as it will go: because Ulysses got Achilles to the war, Achilles' acts are counted as his. Telephus, king of Mysia, was wounded by Achilles' spear and later healed by the rust of that same spear.

sentences.t:
quod Thebae cecidere, meum est, me credite Lesbon,
me Tenedon Chrysenque et Cillan, Apollinis urbes,
et Scyrum cepisse,
sentences.l: that Thebes fell, is mine; believe that I took Lesbos, I Tenedos and Chryse and Cilla, Apollo's towns, and Scyros,
sentences.i: that Thebes fell is my doing; believe that it was I who took Lesbos, I who took Tenedos and Chryse and Cilla, Apollo's towns, and Scyros,
sentences.n: ‘cecidere’ is the poetic third-plural perfect for ‘ceciderunt’; the same ‘-ēre’ perfect returns at 202, 208 and 262 in this part. ‘quod Thebae cecidere’ is a noun clause serving as the subject of ‘est’ — “the fact that Thebes fell is mine”. ‘me ... cepisse’ is an indirect statement after ‘credite’, and ‘me’ is repeated for insistence; ‘Lesbon’, ‘Tenedon’ and ‘Chrysen’ keep their Greek accusative endings.

sentences.t:
mea concussa putate
procubuisse solo Lyrnesia moenia dextra,
sentences.l: reckon that the walls of Lyrnesus, shaken by my right hand, sank down on the ground,
sentences.i: count it that the walls of Lyrnesus were shaken by my right hand and came down to the earth,
sentences.n: Another indirect statement, now after ‘putate’, with ‘moenia’ as its accusative subject and ‘procubuisse’ its infinitive. ‘concussa’ agrees with ‘moenia’ and the ablative of means is split very wide from itself — ‘mea’ stands in 175 and ‘dextra’ at the end of 176, with the whole clause between. ‘solo’ is an ablative of place, “on the ground”.

sentences.t:
utque alias taceam, qui saevum perdere posset
Hectora, nempe dedi: per me iacet inclitus Hector.
sentences.l: and, to say nothing of other towns, the man who could destroy savage Hector — I, surely, gave him: through me famous Hector lies low.
sentences.i: and — to pass over the rest — it was I, surely, who supplied the man who could destroy savage Hector: through me the renowned Hector lies dead.
sentences.n: ‘ut ... taceam’ is praeteritio, the figure of naming a thing by declining to mention it, and Ulysses uses it to keep the catalogue running while claiming to cut it short. ‘qui ... posset’ is a relative clause of characteristic with the subjunctive, “the sort of man who could”; its antecedent is unexpressed and is the object of ‘dedi’. ‘Hectora’ is the Greek accusative. Magnus prints ‘alias’, agreeing with an understood “cities”; some editions print ‘alios’, “other men”.

sentences.t:
Illis haec armis, quibus est inventus Achilles,
arma peto:
sentences.l: For those arms, by which Achilles was found out, I seek these arms:
sentences.i: In exchange for the arms by which Achilles was discovered, I ask for these arms:
sentences.n: ‘illis ... armis’ is an ablative of price, the thing given in exchange: the arms he planted among the women's wares at 165 are what he now offers for the arms of Achilles. ‘haec’ stands at 179 and waits for its noun ‘arma’ at 180, with the relative clause and the whole of ‘illis ... armis’ wrapped around it, so the trade is visible in the word order. ‘inventus’ is “found out, discovered”, picking up the trick of 162–170.

sentences.t: vivo dederam, post fata reposco. —
sentences.l: To him living I had given them; after his fate I ask them back.
sentences.i: I gave them to him living; now that he is dead I ask for them again.
sentences.n: ‘vivo’ is a dative adjective with no noun, standing for Achilles — “to him while he lived”. ‘post fata’ is the poetic plural for the singular, “after his death”. The pluperfect ‘dederam’ set against the present ‘reposco’ makes the whole thing one transaction with a long gap inside it. The em dash the edition prints after ‘reposco’ closes this stretch of the argument before the speech starts again at Aulis.

sentences.t:
Ut dolor unius Danaos pervenit ad omnes
Aulidaque Euboicam complerunt mille carinae,
sentences.l: When the grief of one man reached through to all the Danaans, and a thousand keels had filled Euboean Aulis,
sentences.i: When one man's injury had come home to every Greek, and a thousand ships had filled Euboean Aulis,
sentences.n: ‘ut’ here is temporal with the perfect indicative, “when”, not a purpose word. ‘Aulida’ is a Greek accusative; Aulis lies on the Boeotian coast facing Euboea, which is why it is called ‘Euboicam’. ‘carinae’, properly “keels”, stands for the whole ships. The grief of the one is Menelaus', whom Ulysses turns and addresses by name at 203.

sentences.t:
exspectata diu, nulla aut contraria classi
flamina erant, duraeque iubent Agamemnona sortes
inmeritam saevae natam mactare Dianae.
sentences.l: the breezes, long awaited, were none at all, or against the fleet, and hard lots bid Agamemnon slaughter his undeserving daughter to savage Diana.
sentences.i: the winds, long waited for, either failed or blew against the fleet, and harsh oracles ordered Agamemnon to slaughter his innocent daughter in sacrifice to cruel Diana.
sentences.n: ‘exspectata diu’ agrees with ‘flamina’ across the line-end, and ‘nulla aut contraria’ are predicates of it — the winds “were none or contrary”; ‘classi’ is a dative with ‘contraria’. ‘Agamemnona’ is the Greek accusative. ‘sortes’ are the responses of a lot-oracle. ‘inmeritam’ and ‘saevae’ are Ulysses' own words as he tells it — the girl undeserving, the goddess cruel — and the edition keeps the unassimilated spelling ‘inmeritam’, as it does ‘inmitibus’ at 260.

sentences.t:
Denegat hoc genitor divisque irascitur ipsis
atque in rege tamen pater est.
sentences.l: The father refuses this and grows angry at the very gods, and yet in the king there is a father.
sentences.i: The father refuses, and is angry at the very gods — and even in the king the father is there.
sentences.n: ‘genitor’ near the opening and ‘pater’ near the close are the sentence's whole point: the same man is king and father, and it is the father who answers first. ‘irascitur’ is deponent — passive in form, active in sense — and takes the dative ‘divis ... ipsis’. ‘in rege ... pater est’ uses ‘in’ of a person as the place where something is found, “within the king”.

sentences.t:
Ego mite parentis
ingenium verbis ad publica commoda verti.
sentences.l: I turned the gentle nature of the parent by words to the public advantages.
sentences.i: I turned a father's gentleness round, by argument, to the common good.
sentences.n: ‘verti’ here is the first-person perfect active of ‘verto’, “I turned”, not the present passive infinitive that the same letters could spell; ‘ingenium’ is its object and ‘verbis’ an ablative of means. ‘Ego’ stands first and unemphatic Latin would not need it at all — the pronoun is there to be heard.

sentences.t:
Nunc equidem (fateor, fassoque ignoscat Atrides!)
difficilem tenui sub iniquo iudice causam.
sentences.l: Now indeed — I confess it, and let the son of Atreus pardon the man who has confessed — I maintained a hard case before an unfair judge.
sentences.i: Now I confess it — and may the son of Atreus pardon the man who confesses — I held a difficult brief before a judge set against me.
sentences.n: ‘fasso’ is the perfect participle of the deponent ‘fateor’, active in sense, in the dative with ‘ignoscat’: “let him pardon the one who has confessed”, that is, me. ‘Atrides’ is the Greek patronymic, “son of Atreus”, here Agamemnon. ‘sub iniquo iudice’ is the ablative used of the judge before whom a case is pleaded — and the unfair judge is the very man whose pardon is asked. Magnus prints ‘Nunc’; some editions print ‘hanc’, which would attach to ‘causam’.

sentences.t:
Hunc tamen utilitas populi fraterque datique
summa movet sceptri, laudem ut cum sanguine penset.
sentences.l: Yet the people's advantage and his brother and the sum of the sceptre given him move this man, so that he weighs praise against blood.
sentences.i: Still, the public good and his brother and the whole weight of the sceptre entrusted to him move him, to set glory in the scale against blood.
sentences.n: Three singular subjects with one singular verb, ‘movet’ — Latin regularly lets the verb agree with the nearest subject or treat the group as a single force. ‘dati ... sceptri’ is a perfect participle in the genitive with ‘summa’, “the whole of the sceptre that had been given him”, that is, everything his command amounts to. ‘ut’ is postponed behind ‘laudem’, which is normal in verse; ‘penset’ is its subjunctive, and ‘pensare’ is to weigh one thing against another in a balance.

sentences.t:
Mittor et ad matrem, quae non hortanda, sed astu
decipienda fuit:
sentences.l: I am sent also to the mother, who had to be not urged, but deceived by cunning:
sentences.i: I am sent to the mother too — a woman who had to be not persuaded but outwitted:
sentences.n: ‘hortanda’ and ‘decipienda’ are gerundives with ‘fuit’, the passive periphrastic of obligation: “she was one who had to be…”. ‘Mittor’ is a present passive telling a past event, a historic present, and it is repeated at 196. The mother is Agamemnon's wife, mother of the girl of 185; Ulysses says only that deception was needed, not what the deception was.

sentences.t:
quo si Telamonius isset,
orba suis essent etiamnum lintea ventis.
sentences.l: if the son of Telamon had gone where I went, the sails would even now be bereft of their winds.
sentences.i: if Telamon's son had gone on that errand, the sails would be waiting to this day, with no wind in them.
sentences.n: A contrary-to-fact condition with its two halves in different times: the pluperfect subjunctive ‘isset’ for the past, the imperfect subjunctive ‘essent’ with ‘etiamnum’ for the present — “if he had gone then, they would still be so now”. ‘orba’ takes an ablative of separation, ‘suis ... ventis’. ‘Telamonius’ is the patronymic used as a name, “Telamon's son”; Ulysses uses it again at 266, and ‘Telamoniades’ at 231.

sentences.t:
Mittor et Iliacas audax orator ad arces,
visaque et intrata est altae mihi curia Troiae
(plenaque adhuc erat illa viris),
sentences.l: I am sent also to the citadels of Ilium, a bold spokesman, and the council-house of high Troy was seen and entered by me (and it was still full of men),
sentences.i: I am sent to the towers of Ilium too, and a bold spokesman I was: the council-house of high Troy was seen and entered by me — and it was still crowded with fighting men —
sentences.n: ‘visa et intrata est’ is a compound perfect passive with ‘mihi’ as the dative of agent, which verse allows here where prose would say ‘a me’: “was seen and entered by me”. ‘audax orator’ stands in apposition to the unexpressed “I” of ‘Mittor’. ‘curia’ is the Roman word for a senate-house, laid over the Trojan council, as ‘cives’ is laid over the Greek army at 262. The parenthesis is where the danger of the errand sits.

sentences.t:
interritus egi,
quam mihi mandarat communis Graecia causam,
sentences.l: undaunted I pleaded the case which the whole of Greece in common had entrusted to me,
sentences.i: and undismayed I argued the case that all Greece together had put into my hands,
sentences.n: The antecedent has been drawn inside its own relative clause and left at the end: what Latin says is “I pleaded, which Greece had entrusted to me, the case”. ‘mandarat’ is syncopated for ‘mandaverat’. ‘causam agere’ is the technical phrase for pleading a case in court, and this whole passage is dressed as Roman advocacy. Magnus prints ‘communis’, with Greece; some editions print ‘communem’, taking the adjective with ‘causam’.

sentences.t:
accusoque Parim praedamque Helenamque reposco
et moveo Priamum Priamoque Antenora iunctum.
sentences.l: and I accuse Paris and demand back the plunder and Helen, and I move Priam and Antenor joined to Priam.
sentences.i: and I accuse Paris, and demand back the spoil and Helen with it, and I move Priam, and Antenor at Priam's side.
sentences.n: ‘Parim’ and ‘Antenora’ are Greek accusatives. ‘praedam ... Helenamque’ puts the woman after the goods and in the same list as them. ‘moveo’ is the orator's word, of shifting a hearer's mind; ‘Priamoque ... iunctum’ is a participle with the dative, “joined to Priam”.

sentences.t:
At Paris et fratres et qui rapuere sub illo,
ni tenuere manus (scis hoc, Menelae) nefandas,
sentences.l: But Paris and his brothers and those who did the seizing under him did not hold back their unspeakable hands — you know this, Menelaus —
sentences.i: But Paris and his brothers and the men who did the carrying-off under his lead did not keep their abominable hands to themselves — you know that, Menelaus —
sentences.n: ‘rapuere’ is the poetic third-plural perfect for ‘rapuerunt’, of the raid that carried off the plunder and Helen demanded back at 200. The hands are the Trojans' and the peril is the envoys' own: 204 says that day was the first of the danger Ulysses shared with Menelaus. ‘Menelae’ is a vocative, and Ulysses breaks off to address a man sitting in the audience. Magnus prints ‘ni’, taken as a flat negative, which is hard Latin; some editions print ‘vix’, “scarcely held back”, and the sense of the sentence turns on which is read.

sentences.t: primaque lux nostri tecum fuit illa pericli.
sentences.l: and that light was the first of our danger with you.
sentences.i: and that day was the first of the peril I shared with you.
sentences.n: ‘lux’ is “daylight” standing for “day”, ordinary in verse. ‘nostri ... pericli’ is a genitive with ‘prima’, and ‘pericli’ is the contracted genitive for ‘periculi’. ‘tecum’ keeps Menelaus in the sentence: the danger was the two men's together, which is why the apostrophe of the line before was worth making.

sentences.t:
Longa referre mora est, quae consilioque manuque
utiliter feci spatiosi tempore belli.
sentences.l: It is a long delay to recount the things which I did to good purpose by counsel and by hand in the time of the spacious war.
sentences.i: It would take too long to tell over what I did to good effect, by counsel and by hand, in the long stretch of the war.
sentences.n: ‘longa mora est’ has the infinitive ‘referre’ as its subject — “to recount is a long delay”, that is, it would take too long. This is praeteritio again, cutting the catalogue short while announcing how much of it there is. ‘consilio ... manuque’ pairs head and hand, the two kinds of service this whole trial is about. ‘spatiosi’ is “wide, long drawn out”, of the war's extent in time.

sentences.t:
Post acies primas urbis se moenibus hostes
continuere diu, nec aperti copia Martis
ulla fuit: decimo demum pugnavimus anno.
sentences.l: After the first battle-lines the enemy kept themselves within the city's walls for a long time, and there was no opportunity at all of open war: in the tenth year at last we fought.
sentences.i: After the first engagements the enemy shut themselves up behind the city walls for a long while, and there was no chance whatever of open battle: it was only in the tenth year that we fought.
sentences.n: ‘continuere’ is the ‘-ēre’ perfect for ‘continuerunt’, with ‘se’ — “kept themselves in”. ‘moenibus’ is an ablative of place with no preposition, normal in verse. ‘Mars’ stands by the god's name for war itself, so ‘aperti Martis’ is “open fighting”, and ‘copia’ is “opportunity”. ‘decimo demum ... anno’ answers the ‘diu’ earlier in the sentence: the sentence is built to measure the waiting.

sentences.t:
Quid facis interea, qui nil nisi proelia, nosti?
Quis tuus usus erat?
sentences.l: What are you doing meanwhile, you who know nothing except battles? What use of you was there?
sentences.i: And what were you doing all that while, you who know nothing but fighting? What use were you?
sentences.n: Ulysses turns from the assembly to Ajax himself here, and the second person comes and goes from now on — ‘tu’ again at 224, ‘te’ at 238, third-person ‘iste’ in between; the present ‘facis’ drags the past scene into the moment of the trial. ‘nosti’ is the syncopated perfect ‘novisti’, “you have come to know”, hence “you know”. The edition prints a comma after ‘proelia’, cutting the object off from its own verb ‘nosti’.

sentences.t:
Nam si mea facta requiris,
hostibus insidior, fossas munimine cingo,
sentences.l: For if you ask for my deeds: I lay ambushes for the enemy, I ring the trenches with a rampart,
sentences.i: For if it is my deeds you want: I ambush the enemy, I ring our trenches with earthworks,
sentences.n: ‘insidior’ is deponent — passive in form, active in sense — and takes the dative ‘hostibus’. The present tenses here and down to 215 are historic presents, setting the long middle of the war before the eyes. Magnus prints ‘fossas munimine’, the trenches ringed with a rampart; some editions print ‘fossa munimina’, which turns the case round and makes the ditch the means and the works the thing encircled.

sentences.t:
consolor socios, ut longi taedia belli
mente ferant placida, doceo, quo simus alendi
armandique modo, mittor, quo postulat usus.
sentences.l: I console my comrades, so that they may bear the weariness of the long war with a calm mind; I teach in what way we are to be fed and armed; I am sent wherever need demands.
sentences.i: I hearten my comrades, so that they bear the tedium of a long war with a steady mind; I show how we are to be fed and armed; I am sent wherever the need calls.
sentences.n: ‘ut ... ferant’ is a purpose clause, and ‘mente ... placida’ is an ablative of manner split around its own verb. ‘quo ... modo’ is an indirect question, “in what way”, with its two words held apart across the line-end — ‘quo’ at 214, ‘modo’ at 215 — and ‘simus alendi armandique’ is the passive periphrastic, “we are to be fed and armed”. The three clauses run with no connectives at all, which is the shape of a service-list.

sentences.t:
Ecce Iovis monitu, deceptus imagine somni,
rex iubet incepti curam dimittere belli.
sentences.l: Look — at Jupiter's warning, deceived by the image of a dream, the king orders them to let go the care of the war begun.
sentences.i: Then see: on a warning from Jupiter, taken in by the shape of a dream, the king orders them to give up all care for the war they had begun.
sentences.n: ‘monitu’ is the ablative of a fourth-declension verbal noun found chiefly in that case, “at the warning of”. ‘incepti ... belli’ is a perfect participle in the genitive with ‘curam’, split around it within the line. ‘dimittere’ is an infinitive with ‘iubet’ whose subject is left unexpressed — the men are to give it up. ‘Ecce’ marks the turn to a fresh episode.

sentences.t:
Ille potest auctore suam defendere vocem:
non sinat hoc Aiax delendaque Pergama poscat,
quodque potest, pugnet!
sentences.l: He can defend his own utterance by the one who prompted it: let Ajax not allow this, and let him demand a Pergamum to be destroyed, and — the thing he can do — let him fight!
sentences.i: He at least can plead the authority behind him: let Ajax refuse to allow it, let him call for Troy to be destroyed, and — since it is the one thing he can do — let him fight!
sentences.n: ‘auctore’ stands alone in the ablative and the person meant is left unnamed: “with [Jupiter] as the one who prompted him”, the god named at 216. ‘sinat’, ‘poscat’ and ‘pugnet’ are jussive subjunctives used sarcastically — Ulysses is prescribing what Ajax should have done and did not. ‘delenda ... Pergama’ is a gerundive as the object of ‘poscat’, “a Pergamum-to-be-destroyed”, that is, that it be destroyed.

sentences.t:
Cur non remoratur ituros?
Cur non arma capit? det, quod vaga turba sequatur!
sentences.l: Why does he not hold back the men about to go? Why does he not take up arms? Let him give something for the drifting crowd to follow!
sentences.i: Why does he not stop the men as they set off? Why does he not take up his arms? Let him give the wandering crowd something to follow!
sentences.n: ‘ituros’ is the future participle of ‘eo’ used as a noun, “those about to go”. The two questions are rhetorical and in the present tense, which keeps the old scene in front of the court. ‘quod ... sequatur’ is a relative clause of purpose with the subjunctive, “something for the crowd to follow”. Magnus prints the jussive ‘det’; some editions print the indicative ‘dat’, which would make it a statement rather than a demand.

sentences.t: Non erat hoc nimium numquam nisi magna loquenti.
sentences.l: This was not too much for a man speaking never anything except great things.
sentences.i: That would have been no great matter for one who never talks of anything but great things.
sentences.n: ‘loquenti’ is a dative participle with no noun, “for one speaking”, and ‘numquam nisi magna’ is its object, “never anything except great things”. ‘non erat nimium’ is the plain imperfect indicative where English wants “would not have been” — Latin states what was within reach as a fact rather than as a condition. The barb is at Ajax's way of talking, and the line lands it without naming him.

sentences.t:
Quid quod et ipse fugit? Vidi, puduitque videre,
cum tu terga dares inhonestaque vela parares.
sentences.l: What of the fact that he too fled, himself? I saw it, and it shamed me to see, when you were giving your back and making ready dishonourable sails.
sentences.i: And what of this — that he ran himself? I saw it, and was ashamed to see it, when you turned your back and were getting the shameful sails ready.
sentences.n: ‘quid quod’ is a formula of argument, “what of the fact that…”, bringing on a further charge. ‘puduit’ is impersonal, “it caused shame”, with the person shamed in the accusative and here left unexpressed. Across the two sentences Ulysses swings from speaking of Ajax in the third person (‘fugit’) to addressing him in the second (‘tu ... dares ... parares’), and the swing is the sting. ‘terga dare’ is the set phrase for turning to run.

sentences.t:
Nec mora, “quid facitis? quae vos dementia” dixi
“concitat, o socii? captam dimittite Troiam!
Quidve domum fertis decimo, nisi dedecus, anno?”
sentences.l: And no delay: “What are you doing? what madness,” I said, “drives you on, comrades? Let a captured Troy go! or what are you carrying home in the tenth year, if not disgrace?”
sentences.i: And at once: “What are you about? What madness,” I said, “is driving you, comrades? Throw away a Troy already taken! And what do you carry home in the tenth year, if not disgrace?”
sentences.n: ‘nec mora’ is an ellipse — “and [there was] no delay”. As at 168 the edition breaks the quotation to insert the verb of saying, so the reported words run on both sides of ‘dixi’. ‘captam dimittite Troiam’ is an ironic imperative: he orders them to do the thing he is stopping, and ‘captam’ concedes the city as already taken. ‘decimo ... anno’ picks up the tenth year of 209. Magnus prints the imperative ‘dimittite’; some editions print the infinitive ‘dimittere’.

sentences.t:
Talibus atque aliis, in quae dolor ipse disertum
fecerat, aversos profuga de classe reduxi.
sentences.l: By such words and others, for which grief itself had made me eloquent, I led back the men who had turned away, from the fleet in flight.
sentences.i: With these words and others, for which grief itself had made me eloquent, I brought back the men who had turned away, from a fleet already running.
sentences.n: ‘talibus atque aliis’ is an ablative of means with its noun, “words”, left to be supplied from the sense. ‘in quae’ is “with a view to which”, marking the field in which the eloquence worked. ‘profuga ... classe’ transfers the epithet from the men to the ships — the fleet itself is called a runaway. ‘aversos’ is a participle used as a noun, “the men who had turned away”.

sentences.t: Convocat Atrides socios terrore paventes;
sentences.l: The son of Atreus calls together his comrades, quaking with terror;
sentences.i: The son of Atreus summons his comrades, trembling with fright;
sentences.n: ‘Atrides’ is the Greek patronymic again, as at 189, and here it is Agamemnon. ‘terrore’ is an ablative of cause with ‘paventes’, which agrees with ‘socios’ and not with the king. The present ‘convocat’ keeps the historic-present telling that runs through the whole episode.

sentences.t:
nec Telamoniades etiam nunc hiscere quicquam
audet, at ausus erat reges incessere dictis
Thersites etiam, per me haud impune protervus!
sentences.l: and the son of Telamon does not even then dare to utter anything, but Thersites even had dared to assail kings with words — insolent, and by my doing not unpunished!
sentences.i: and Telamon's son does not, even then, dare so much as open his mouth — yet Thersites had dared to attack kings with his words, and his insolence did not go unpunished, thanks to me.
sentences.n: ‘hiscere’ is “to open the mouth, gape”, so “to utter a syllable”, with ‘quicquam’ as its object. The present ‘audet’ set against the pluperfect ‘ausus erat’ — from the semi-deponent ‘audeo’, active in sense — puts Ajax's silence beside Thersites' earlier daring. ‘per me haud impune protervus’ is a nominative phrase in apposition to ‘Thersites’, and ‘haud ... impune’ is litotes, a denial standing in for a strong positive. Magnus prints ‘haud impune protervus’, of the man; some editions print ‘haut inpune protervis’, taking the adjective with ‘dictis’, “with insolent words”.

sentences.t:
Erigor et trepidos cives exhortor in hostem
amissamque mea virtutem voce reposco.
sentences.l: I raise myself up and urge the trembling citizens on against the enemy, and I demand back their lost courage by my voice.
sentences.i: I rise up and urge the frightened men on against the enemy, and with my voice I call their lost courage back.
sentences.n: ‘Erigor’ is passive in form used reflexively, “I lift myself up”. ‘reposco’ is the same verb as at 180: this speech keeps demanding back what was once given. In 235 the two pairs interlock — ‘amissam ... virtutem’ with ‘mea’ inside it, and ‘mea ... voce’ with ‘virtutem’ inside that. ‘cives’ is a Roman word for fellow-citizens laid over the Greek army, as ‘curia’ was laid over the Trojan council at 197. Magnus prints ‘reposco’, “I demand back”; some editions print ‘repono’, “I put back”.

sentences.t:
Tempore ab hoc, quodcumque potest fecisse videri
fortiter iste, meum est, qui dantem terga retraxi.
sentences.l: From this time on, whatever that man there can be seen to have done bravely is mine — I, who dragged him back as he was giving his back.
sentences.i: From that moment, whatever that fellow can be thought to have done bravely belongs to me, who hauled him back when he was in flight.
sentences.n: ‘iste’ is the contemptuous demonstrative, “that man there”, as ‘isto’ was at 157. ‘potest ... videri fecisse’ is a personal passive — “he can be seen to have done” — where English prefers “it can be seen that he did”. ‘dantem terga’ is a participle used as a noun and picks up ‘terga dares’ at 224, the same charge now stated as accomplished fact. ‘qui ... retraxi’ is a relative clause with a first-person verb, picking up the “me” inside ‘meum’: “mine, who dragged him back”.

sentences.t: Denique de Danais quis te laudatve petitve?
sentences.l: In short, of the Danaans who praises you or seeks you out?
sentences.i: In a word: which of the Greeks praises you, or asks for you?
sentences.n: The doubled ‘-ve ... -ve’ is “either… or”, attached to the ends of both verbs. ‘petit’ here is not “attack” but “seeks out, asks for” — the sense the next lines fill in, where Diomedes chooses Ulysses as his companion. ‘Danais’ is one of the epic names for the Greeks, ablative with ‘de’.

sentences.t:
At sua Tydides mecum communicat acta,
me probat et socio semper confidit Ulixe.
sentences.l: But the son of Tydeus shares his own doings with me, approves of me, and is always confident, with Ulysses as his ally.
sentences.i: But the son of Tydeus shares his exploits with me, thinks well of me, and is always sure of himself when Ulysses is at his side.
sentences.n: ‘Tydides’ is the Greek patronymic, “son of Tydeus”, and the man is named outright as Diomedes at 242. ‘socio ... Ulixe’ is a verbless ablative absolute, “with Ulysses as ally” — Latin has no present participle of “to be”, so the construction simply does without one. The same two words can equally be taken as the ablative complement of ‘confidit’, “trusts in Ulysses as his ally”, and the Latin does not decide between them. Ulysses names himself in the third person, which the shape of the boast requires.

sentences.t:
Est aliquid, de tot Graiorum milibus unum
a Diomede legi (nec me sors ire iubebat !),
sentences.l: It is something, to be chosen out of so many thousands of Greeks, one man, by Diomedes — and no lot was ordering me to go!
sentences.i: It counts for something to have been picked out by Diomedes, one man from so many thousands of Greeks — and it was no drawing of lots that sent me!
sentences.n: ‘est aliquid’ is “it is something”, that is, no small matter, and the passive infinitive ‘legi’ is its subject, with ‘unum’ agreeing with the unexpressed accusative “me”. ‘sors’ is the lot: dangerous errands were assigned by drawing, so the parenthesis claims the choice was made on merit and not by chance. The edition prints a space between ‘iubebat’ and the exclamation mark inside the parenthesis.

sentences.t:
si tamen et spreto noctisque hostisque periclo
ausum eadem, quae nos, Phrygia de gente Dolona
interimo,
sentences.l: if, though, the danger both of the night and of the enemy having been despised, I kill Dolon of the Phrygian race, who had dared the same things as we,
sentences.i: if, that is, it counts too that — the danger of the night and of the enemy scorned — I killed Dolon, a man of Phrygian stock who had dared the same errand as we had,
sentences.n: ‘spreto ... periclo’ is an ablative absolute, “the danger having been despised”, with ‘noctisque hostisque’ a double genitive depending on ‘periclo’. ‘ausum eadem, quae nos’ agrees with ‘Dolona’ and is the participle of the semi-deponent ‘audeo’, active in sense: “having dared the same things as we”. ‘Dolona’ is a Greek accusative. ‘interimo’ is a historic present in a clause reaching back to ‘est aliquid’ at 241 — “and it is something too, if…”. Magnus prints ‘si’; some editions print ‘sic’.

sentences.t:
non ante tamen, quam cuncta coegi
prodere, et edidici, quid perfida Troia pararet.
sentences.l: not, however, before I had forced him to betray everything, and had learned right through what treacherous Troy was preparing.
sentences.i: though not before I had forced him to give up everything, and had learned in full what treacherous Troy was planning.
sentences.n: ‘non ante ... quam’ is ‘antequam’ split in two, “not before”. The perfects ‘coegi’ and ‘edidici’ stand against the historic present ‘interimo’ just before, so that the killing is reported as if happening now and the interrogation as already finished. ‘quid ... pararet’ is an indirect question with the imperfect subjunctive. ‘edidici’ is from ‘ediscere’, “to learn a thing right through”, and ‘perfida’ is Ulysses' word for the city, not a neutral epithet.

sentences.t:
Omnia cognoram, nec, quod specularer, habebam,
et iam promissa poteram cum laude reverti.
sentences.l: I had come to know everything, and I had nothing that I might spy out, and already I could return with the praise that had been promised.
sentences.i: I had found out everything; there was nothing left for me to spy on, and I could already have gone back with the credit I had been promised.
sentences.n: ‘cognoram’ is syncopated for ‘cognoveram’. ‘quod specularer’ is a relative clause of characteristic with the subjunctive, “anything of a kind to spy out”, and its antecedent is left unexpressed. ‘poteram ... reverti’ is the imperfect indicative where English wants “could have returned”: Latin states the possibility as a fact instead of hedging it. ‘promissa ... laude’ is split by ‘poteram cum’, the preposition standing inside the pair as Latin regularly allows.

sentences.t:
Haud contentus eo petii tentoria Rhesi
inque suis ipsum castris comitesque peremi
atque ita captivo victor votisque potitus
ingredior curru laetos imitante triumphos;
sentences.l: Not content with that, I made for the tents of Rhesus, and in his own camp I killed the man himself and his companions, and so, a victor, having got possession of a captive chariot and of what I had prayed for, I ride in, the chariot mimicking glad triumphs;
sentences.i: Not content with that, I made for Rhesus' tents, and killed the man himself and his men in his own camp, and so, victorious and in possession of the captured chariot and of everything I had prayed for, I ride in with the chariot playing at a triumph;
sentences.n: ‘potitus’ is the perfect participle of the deponent ‘potior’, active in sense and governing the ablative — ‘captivo ... curru votisque’; ‘captivo’ at 251 has no noun until ‘curru’ at 252. The same ‘curru ... imitante triumphos’ then works as an ablative absolute, “the chariot imitating glad triumphs”, so the one word does double duty. ‘peremi’ takes both ‘ipsum’ and ‘comites’. The triumph is a Roman ceremony, and Ovid lets Ulysses reach for it in the Greek camp.

sentences.t:
cuius equos pretium pro nocte poposcerat hostis,
arma negate mihi, fueritque benignior Aiax!
sentences.l: The man whose horses the enemy had demanded as payment for a night — deny me his arms, and let Ajax have been the kinder!
sentences.i: Deny me the arms of the man whose horses the enemy had asked as his wage for that night — and then let Ajax be the one who turns out the more generous!
sentences.n: The relative clause runs ahead of its antecedent: ‘cuius’ looks forward to the owner of the ‘arma’ in the next line, Achilles, whose horses the enemy — Dolon, killed at 245 — had asked as his fee. ‘pretium’ is in apposition to ‘equos’, “the horses as a price”. ‘negate’ is an ironic imperative, and the perfect subjunctive ‘fuerit’ is a concession granted with a sneer: refuse me, and even Ajax will have proved the kinder of you.

sentences.t:
Quid Lycii referam Sarpedonis agmina ferro
devastata meo?
sentences.l: Why should I recount the ranks of Lycian Sarpedon, laid waste by my iron?
sentences.i: Why should I tell over the companies of Lycian Sarpedon, laid waste by my steel?
sentences.n: ‘quid referam’ is a deliberative subjunctive, “why am I to recount?”, and it is praeteritio once more — the question is put so that the catalogue can follow anyway. ‘ferro’ is “with iron”, the metal standing for the weapon. ‘Lycii ... Sarpedonis’ is split around the verb, and ‘agmina’ at 255 waits for ‘devastata’ at 256 across the line-end.

sentences.t:
Cum multo sanguine fudi
Coeranon Iphitiden et Alastoraque Chromiumque
Alcandrumque Haliumque Noemonaque Prytanimque,
sentences.l: With much blood I laid low Coeranus son of Iphitus, and Alastor and Chromius, and Alcandrus and Halius and Noëmon and Prytanis,
sentences.i: With much bloodshed I struck down Coeranus the son of Iphitus, and Alastor and Chromius, Alcandrus and Halius, Noëmon and Prytanis,
sentences.n: ‘Iphitiden’ is a Greek patronymic in the accusative, “son of Iphitus”. The names in the roll mix Greek accusative endings — ‘Coeranon’, ‘Alastora’, ‘Noemona’ — with Latin ones — ‘Chromium’, ‘Alcandrum’, ‘Halium’. The ‘-que’ hung on name after name is polysyndeton, a deliberate piling-up that makes the roll feel longer than it is. ‘fudi’ is from ‘fundo’, “pour out”, used of laying men low.

sentences.t:
exitioque dedi cum Chersidamante Thoona
et Charopem fatisque inmitibus Ennomon actum
quique minus celebres nostra sub moenibus urbis
procubuere manu.
sentences.l: and I gave over to destruction Thoön along with Chersidamas, and Charops, and Ennomus driven on by pitiless fates, and those less renowned who fell beneath the walls of the city by my hand.
sentences.i: and I handed over to death Thoön together with Chersidamas, and Charops, and Ennomus, driven by pitiless fates — and men less famous, who went down by my hand under the city's walls.
sentences.n: ‘exitio dedi’ has a dative of purpose, “gave over to destruction”. ‘actum’ agrees with ‘Ennomon’, with ‘fatis inmitibus’ the force driving him; the edition keeps the unassimilated ‘inmitibus’, as it kept ‘inmeritam’ at 185. ‘procubuere’ is the ‘-ēre’ perfect for ‘procubuerunt’. ‘quique’ is ‘qui’ with ‘-que’, “and those who”, its antecedent unexpressed and drawn into the run of objects. ‘nostra’ stands at 261 and its noun ‘manu’ at 262, with ‘sub moenibus urbis procubuere’ lying between them.

sentences.t:
Sunt et mihi vulnera, cives,
ipso pulchra loco; nec vanis credite verbis:
sentences.l: There are wounds to me too, citizens — beautiful by their very place; and do not believe empty words:
sentences.i: I have wounds too, citizens — and beautiful ones, by the very place they are in. Do not take words on trust:
sentences.n: ‘sunt ... mihi vulnera’ is the dative of possession, “there are wounds to me” for “I have wounds” — the same construction as the pedigree at 144–145. ‘ipso ... loco’ is an ablative of respect, “beautiful in the very place”: a wound in front is honourable and one in the back is not, which is the charge he made at 224 and again at 237. ‘cives’ is a vocative and turns him back to the assembly after the long address to Ajax. ‘nec ... credite’ is a negative command made with ‘nec’ rather than with ‘noli’.

sentences.t:
adspicite en!” vestemque manu deduxit et “haec sunt
pectora semper” ait “vestris exercita rebus.
sentences.l: look, here!” — and he drew his garment down with his hand — and “this breast,” he says, “has always been worn hard in your affairs.
sentences.i: look — see!” and he drew his robe down with his hand, and “this breast,” he says, “has always been worked hard in your service.
sentences.n: The outer narrator breaks into the speech for half a line: ‘vestemque manu deduxit’ is reported of Ulysses from outside, in the third person, and the edition's quotation marks show the seam on either side of it. ‘pectora’ is the poetic plural for a single breast, and ‘exercita’ agrees with it; ‘vestris ... rebus’ is the ablative with it, “worn hard by your affairs”. Magnus prints ‘deduxit’, “drew down”; some editions print ‘diduxit’, “drew apart”.

sentences.t:
At nil impendit per tot Telamonius annos
sanguinis in socios et habet sine vulnere corpus!
sentences.l: But the son of Telamon has spent nothing of blood on his comrades through so many years, and has a body without a wound!
sentences.i: But Telamon's son has spent not a drop of blood on his comrades in all these years, and his body has not a wound on it!
sentences.n: ‘nil ... sanguinis’ is a partitive genitive with the neuter ‘nil’, “nothing of blood”, and the two are held apart across the line-end, ‘nil’ near the head of 266 and ‘sanguinis’ the first word of 267. ‘impendit’ is the same in the present and the perfect, and ‘per tot ... annos’ makes “has spent” the natural reading. ‘Telamonius’ is the patronymic again, as at 194, and the speech ends on the contrast the bared breast was shown for.
